author: A Robot
objectives: Describe the observed apparent path of Mars during a retrograde episode: eastward drift, stationary point, westward loop, second stationary point, and return to eastward drift.
Explain apparent retrograde motion of an outer planet as a heliocentric line-of-sight effect caused when faster-moving Earth overtakes the slower outer planet.
Contrast the geocentric epicycle explanation with the heliocentric explanation and explain why the heliocentric model is preferred for parsimony.
Predict that retrograde motion for an outer planet occurs near opposition, when Earth is between the Sun and the outer planet and is overtaking it.
Compare Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn retrograde loops and explain why more distant planets show smaller loops.

modules.moduleName: Scene 1: Mars Reverses Against the Stars
modules.description: Students observe a six-month time-lapse of Mars moving against labeled ecliptic constellations, including the characteristic retrograde loop.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify Mars as a moving red point against a nearly fixed star background.
Describe the sequence of prograde motion, stationary points, retrograde motion, and resumed prograde motion.
Recognize the observed reversal as the historical puzzle that motivated competing planetary models.
instructions: Face the curved starfield panel in front of you.
Advance through the clips and compare Mars with the constellation labels.
Use the trail and arrow direction to describe the apparent path.

components.text: Leo        Virgo        Libra        Scorpius
Month 0: Mars among the ecliptic stars
Month 0: Mars starts west of Virgo

clips.changeMeaning: Mars begins as a red point against labeled ecliptic constellations, establishing the observational frame for apparent planetary motion.
clips.narration: Begin from Earth's night sky. The distant stars form an almost fixed background, while Mars changes position from night to night along the ecliptic.

components.text: Months 1-2: eastward prograde drift

clips.changeMeaning: Mars shifts eastward and a short blue trail appears to show normal prograde drift before the reversal begins.
clips.narration: For about two months, Mars drifts slowly eastward against the stars. This ordinary apparent motion is called prograde motion.

components.text: First stationary point: Mars seems to pause

clips.changeMeaning: Mars reaches a turning point and the arrow becomes small and yellow, indicating apparent motion has nearly stopped.
clips.narration: Mars then slows until it seems nearly stationary. This turning point is called a stationary point, and it marks the start of the reversal.

components.text: Months 3-4: westward retrograde loop, about 15 degrees

clips.changeMeaning: Mars moves westward and the trail expands into a red loop, revealing the apparent retrograde path against the constellations.
clips.narration: For roughly two months, Mars appears to move westward. The trail marks a retrograde loop about fifteen degrees wide on the sky.

components.text: Month 6: eastward motion resumes - why did Mars reverse?

clips.changeMeaning: Mars moves eastward beyond the completed loop, leaving the full trail visible as the central puzzle for explanation.
clips.narration: After a second stationary point, Mars resumes eastward motion. Why would a planet seem to stop, reverse, and start again? That puzzle shaped the history of astronomy.

modules.description: An Earth-centered deferent-and-epicycle model reproduces the retrograde loop while revealing the tuned machinery required.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Define deferent and epicycle in a geocentric model.
Explain how combined circular motions can make Mars appear to reverse as seen from Earth.
Evaluate the geocentric explanation as observationally useful but mechanically complex.
instructions: View the Earth-centered tabletop model from above.
Follow the epicycle center on the large ring and Mars on the small ring.
Notice how the inner epicycle segment creates the apparent reversal.

components.text: Geocentric model: deferent plus epicycle
Earth fixed at center: Mars uses deferent plus epicycle

clips.changeMeaning: The Earth-centered deferent and smaller epicycle are labeled implicitly so students can identify the model's geometric parts.
clips.narration: In the geocentric model, Earth sits at the center. Mars rides on a small circle called an epicycle, whose center rides on a larger circle called the deferent.

components.text: Two circular motions are carefully combined

clips.changeMeaning: The epicycle center and Mars move to a new location, showing that two circular motions are combined to make the apparent path.
clips.narration: The model adds two circular motions: motion of the epicycle center around Earth and motion of Mars around the epicycle center.

components.text: Inner epicycle segment can create apparent backward motion

clips.changeMeaning: Mars is placed on the inner side of the epicycle, where its motion can make the sightline sweep backward from Earth.
clips.narration: When Mars is on the inner side of the epicycle, closest to Earth, its epicycle motion can temporarily make the line of sight sweep backward.

components.text: Works geometrically, but requires tuned extra machinery

clips.changeMeaning: The label emphasizes that the model can fit the observation but requires tuned sizes and speeds for each planet.
clips.narration: This explanation can reproduce retrograde loops, but it requires carefully tuned sizes and speeds. Better data often required added epicycles, making the model increasingly elaborate.

modules.description: A Sun-centered tabletop model shows Earth and Mars moving on smooth orbits, revealing retrograde as an overtaking effect.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: State that Earth orbits at 1 AU in 1 year while Mars orbits at about 1.52 AU in 1.88 years.
Explain why Earth overtakes Mars roughly every 26 months.
Distinguish physical orbital motion from apparent sky motion.
instructions: Look down on the Sun-centered model.
Follow Earth on the inner orbit and Mars on the outer orbit.
Notice that neither planet physically loops backward.

components.text: Heliocentric model: smooth orbits around the Sun
Sun-centered view: Earth inside, Mars outside

clips.changeMeaning: The Sun-centered orbits appear with Earth inside Mars, establishing a heliocentric reference frame for the same event.
clips.narration: Now view the solar system from above. In the heliocentric model, Earth and Mars both orbit the Sun on separate paths.

components.text: Earth: 1 AU, 1 year; Mars: 1.52 AU, 1.88 years

clips.changeMeaning: Earth advances through a larger angle than Mars, demonstrating the faster motion of the inner planet around the Sun.
clips.narration: Earth is closer to the Sun and completes an orbit in one year. Mars is farther out and takes about 1.88 years, so Earth gains on Mars.

components.text: Retrograde season: Earth overtakes Mars near opposition

clips.changeMeaning: Earth is placed between the Sun and Mars, highlighting the opposition geometry associated with retrograde motion.
clips.narration: About every 26 months, Earth catches up to and overtakes Mars on the inside track. Near this time, Earth lies between the Sun and Mars, called opposition.

components.text: No epicycles needed: two smooth heliocentric orbits

clips.changeMeaning: The planets continue to new smooth-orbit positions while the highlight fades, emphasizing that Mars is not physically looping.
clips.narration: From outside the solar system, Mars never loops backward. The apparent loop is produced by observing Mars from a moving Earth.

modules.moduleName: Scene 4: Linking Orbit Geometry to the Sky
modules.description: A split view connects the heliocentric model to the Earth-sky view using a line of sight from Earth through Mars to the star background.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Trace the line of sight from Earth through Mars to a projected sky position.
Relate the reversal of the line-of-sight sweep to Mars's retrograde path.
Explain that retrograde motion is an apparent motion caused by real geometry.
instructions: Compare the orbit model on the left with the sky panel on the right.
Follow the white line from Earth through Mars to the projected Mars dot.
Watch how the projected dot reverses when Earth overtakes Mars.

components.text: Line of sight connects orbit geometry to the sky path

clips.changeMeaning: The split view appears with a sightline from Earth through Mars and an initial projected Mars position on the sky panel.
clips.narration: Here the outside view and sky view appear together. The white line shows the observer's line of sight from Earth through Mars to the background stars.

clips.changeMeaning: Before overtaking, Earth and Mars advance and the projected Mars dot shifts eastward on the sky panel to show prograde motion.
clips.narration: Before Earth overtakes Mars, the line of sight sweeps eastward through the constellations. The sky panel shows Mars's normal prograde drift.

clips.changeMeaning: During the overtake, the sightline changes direction and the projected Mars dot moves westward, matching the retrograde segment.
clips.narration: As Earth passes Mars, the line of sight reverses direction. On the sky panel, Mars retraces part of its path westward: the retrograde segment.

components.text: Changing line of sight produces the apparent loop

clips.changeMeaning: After the overtake, the sightline and projected dot resume eastward motion, completing the geometric explanation of the loop.
clips.narration: After Earth has passed, the line of sight resumes its eastward sweep. Retrograde is not a flaw in the eye; it is apparent motion caused by real changing geometry.

modules.description: Students physically or virtually move around a floor orbit while watching Mars against a star strip, experiencing retrograde as a viewpoint effect.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Experience how observer motion changes an object's apparent position against distant background stars.
Connect closest approach to the most noticeable apparent reversal.
Use the passing-car analogy to explain apparent backward drift.
instructions: If space permits, step slowly along the glowing floor orbit; otherwise use Next to simulate positions.
Keep Mars in view against the distant star labels.
Notice the apparent reversal near closest approach.

components.text: Move along Earth's orbit while watching Mars
Start: Mars appears left of center

clips.changeMeaning: The floor orbit and initial student marker establish that the learner represents Earth's moving viewpoint.
clips.narration: Now your body represents the observing Earth. Mars is farther away against the star strip. Your position changes the direction in which Mars appears.

components.text: Before closest approach: apparent position drifts eastward

clips.changeMeaning: The student marker advances on the inner orbit and the apparent sky marker shifts eastward, simulating the prograde portion.
clips.narration: Before closest approach, moving along the inner orbit makes Mars appear to drift across the star labels in the prograde direction.

components.text: Closest approach: apparent motion reverses westward

clips.changeMeaning: At closest approach the flag appears and the apparent marker shifts backward, making the reversal a direct result of observer motion.
clips.narration: Near closest approach, your viewing angle changes rapidly. Mars appears to move backward relative to the distant stars, even though Mars itself is not reversing.

components.text: After passing: eastward motion resumes

clips.changeMeaning: The student marker moves past closest approach and the apparent marker resumes eastward motion, completing the embodied sequence.
clips.narration: After you pass, the apparent motion resumes. This is like passing a slower car: from your moving viewpoint, the other car can seem to drift backward.

modules.moduleName: Scene 6: Comparing Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn
modules.description: An expanded heliocentric scene compares the apparent retrograde loop sizes of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Compare approximate loop sizes: Mars about 15 degrees, Jupiter about 10 degrees, and Saturn about 7 degrees.
Explain why more distant planets show smaller apparent loops.
Apply parallax-style reasoning to outer-planet retrograde motion.
instructions: Inspect the expanded solar-system model and loop comparison panel.
Step through the highlighted planets one at a time.
Relate loop size to the planet's distance from Earth and the Sun.

components.text: Retrograde loop size decreases with distance
Same cause, different loop sizes

clips.changeMeaning: The expanded model and loop panel appear with all three outer planets, setting up a distance-based comparison.
clips.narration: All outer planets can show retrograde motion. Here Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn are compared in one heliocentric view.

components.text: Mars: largest loop, about 15 degrees

clips.changeMeaning: Mars and the largest loop icon brighten, showing that nearby Mars has the largest apparent retrograde loop in the comparison.
clips.narration: Mars is relatively close during opposition, so Earth's orbital motion produces a large change in line of sight. Its loop is about fifteen degrees across.

components.text: Jupiter: smaller loop, about 10 degrees

clips.changeMeaning: Jupiter and its medium loop icon brighten, connecting greater distance with a smaller apparent loop.
clips.narration: Jupiter is farther away, about 5.2 astronomical units from the Sun. The same Earth motion subtends a smaller angle, so the loop is about ten degrees.

components.text: Saturn: smallest here, about 7 degrees

clips.changeMeaning: Saturn and the smallest loop icon brighten, showing that still greater distance produces an even smaller apparent loop.
clips.narration: Saturn is farther still, about 9.5 astronomical units. Earth's orbital baseline shifts the line of sight even less, so the loop is about seven degrees.

components.text: Farther planet -> smaller apparent retrograde loop

clips.changeMeaning: All loop icons become visible together with a rule statement, reinforcing the parallax-style relationship between distance and apparent shift.
clips.narration: This is a parallax-style rule: nearby objects shift more when you move, while distant objects shift less. Farther outer planets make smaller retrograde loops.

modules.description: A guided prediction scene asks students to place Mars near opposition for two different Earth positions, using a sky inset as feedback.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Predict that Mars retrograde occurs near opposition when Earth is between the Sun and Mars.
Use relative geometry rather than absolute position to identify retrograde configurations.
Transfer the opposition rule to a second Earth position.
instructions: Drag or mentally place Mars on its orbit near the highlighted opposition region.
Use the sky inset to decide whether the configuration would show retrograde motion.
Repeat for the second Earth position.

components.text: Challenge: where must Mars be for retrograde?
Find where Earth is about to overtake Mars

clips.changeMeaning: The Sun-Earth-Mars prediction setup appears with Mars away from opposition and the inset showing no retrograde loop yet.
clips.narration: Now predict the geometry. Earth is fixed on its orbit. Place Mars where an observer on Earth would soon see retrograde motion.

components.text: Hint: align Sun, Earth, and Mars near opposition

clips.changeMeaning: A yellow arc appears opposite the Sun from Earth, cueing the near-opposition region for retrograde prediction.
clips.narration: Hint: retrograde for an outer planet occurs near opposition, when Earth is on the inside track between the Sun and the planet.

components.text: Confirmed: retrograde occurs near opposition

clips.changeMeaning: Mars is moved into the valid opposition region; the arc turns green and the inset displays a retrograde loop.
clips.narration: Correct. With Mars near this direction, Earth is poised to overtake it, and the inset shows the retrograde loop that would be recorded against the stars.

components.text: Repeat: find opposition for this new Earth position

clips.changeMeaning: Earth is moved to a different orbital location and the feedback resets, requiring students to apply the same relative rule again.
clips.narration: Now Earth is at a different point in its orbit. The correct absolute location changes, but the relative rule stays the same.

components.text: Confirmed again: relative geometry controls retrograde

clips.changeMeaning: Mars is placed in the new opposition region, confirming that retrograde depends on relative alignment rather than fixed location.
clips.narration: Yes. Again Earth is on the inner orbit, aligned with Mars, and ready to pass it. Retrograde depends on relative geometry, not a special absolute location.

modules.description: A closing summary highlights the observed phenomenon, geocentric epicycles, heliocentric resolution, linked viewpoints, and outer-planet comparison.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Summarize the five major concepts from the lab.
Differentiate physical orbital motion from apparent sky motion.
State a concise explanation for outer-planet retrograde motion.
instructions: Read each highlighted summary item as the narration reviews it.
Use the final sentence as a model for explaining retrograde motion in your own words.

components.text: Retrograde Motion: Key Ideas

1. Mars: eastward -> westward loop -> eastward
2. Geocentric epicycles can reproduce the loop
3. Heliocentric orbits explain it naturally
4. Line of sight links orbit geometry to sky motion
5. Farther outer planets make smaller loops
Earth overtakes a slower outer planet, changing the line of sight.
Observed pattern: prograde, stationary, retrograde, stationary, prograde

clips.changeMeaning: The first summary area is highlighted to review the observed sky pattern that began the lab.
clips.narration: First, the observed pattern: Mars drifts eastward, slows, moves westward in a loop, and then resumes eastward motion.

components.text: Geocentric model: predictive, but increasingly elaborate

clips.changeMeaning: The highlight moves to the geocentric idea, reviewing epicycles as a workable but complex explanation.
clips.narration: Second, geocentric astronomy used epicycles on deferents. This reproduced the loop but required tuned extra machinery.

components.text: Heliocentric model: Earth overtakes slower Mars

clips.changeMeaning: The highlight moves to the heliocentric idea, reviewing Earth overtaking Mars as the simpler physical explanation.
clips.narration: Third, the heliocentric model explains the event with smooth orbits. Earth moves faster on the inner orbit and overtakes Mars.

components.text: The loop is apparent sky motion caused by real geometry

clips.changeMeaning: The highlight moves to the line-of-sight idea, reinforcing the connection between external geometry and apparent sky path.
clips.narration: Fourth, the line of sight links the outside view to the sky view. As Earth passes Mars, the projected position against the stars reverses.

components.text: Final: Earth overtakes a slower outer planet, so its apparent position shifts backward against the stars.

clips.changeMeaning: The final idea is highlighted and a concise final explanation is displayed for students to retain.
clips.narration: Finally, all outer planets retrograde for the same reason, but more distant planets make smaller loops. In one sentence: Earth overtakes a slower outer planet, causing the line of sight to sweep backward across the stars.
